newsitem.title: USA: Bernstein recommends CIGNA on investor call.
newsitem.headline: Bernstein recommends CIGNA on investor call.

text.p: Sanford C. Bernstein analyst Weston Hicks said he told a group of about 100 investors on a conference call Friday that he believes concerns about CIGNA Corp's property-casualty business are overblown and said he believes the stock is cheap.
Hicks said he believes CIGNA's shares are worth about $200, with the company's performance fueled by its strong healthcare business.
CIGNA shares rose 4-1/8, or nearly three percent, to 154-1/2 at midday amid general strength in the financial sector.

CIGNA's restructuring of its property-casualty business was dealt a setback earlier this week when a court rejected regulatory approval of the transaction and ordered CIGNA back to regulators for a new hearing.
But, Hicks said, the property-casualty business represents a small part of CIGNA's overall operations.
"People are obsessing over eight percent of their business," Hicks said of CIGNA's property-casualty business.

CIGNA last year split its domestic property-casualty business into two separate units, one for the profitable, ongoing business and a separate runoff for the unprofitable, discontinued business, stemming mostly from asbestos and environmental claims.
Opponents of CIGNA's restructuring have argued that the runoff may not have enough capital to pay all future claims.
But, Hicks said, "at the end of the day, there's a very strong case to be made that they're economically, adequately reserved for environmental and asbestos."
Hicks also said the runoff businesses at CIGNA and The Hartford are not at all comparable to the troubled runoff business of Home Insurance Co.

The Home, the principal subsidiary of Home Holdings Inc, was placed under formal state supervision on Tuesday after a decline in its risk-based capital, raising concerns about the capital adequacy of other runoffs.
Sweden's Trygg-Hansa/SPP Holding AB is a majority shareholder in Home Holdings and Zurich Insurance Co has an equity position and warrants to purchase more.

"We did some analysis of Home Insurance versus CIGNA versus Hartford and we found that if you think Hartford and CIGNA are in the same situation as Home in terms of the runoff business, you just haven't done your analysis," he said.
As of 1995, Hicks said, CIGNA had $1.7 billion in reserves earmarked for future claims on business written in 1986 and prior, while Home had no such reserves.

"The Home was restructured as a last ditch effort when it was going to fail anyway," Hicks said. "CIGNA was restructured as it's improving, while it has this tremendously profitable other part of the business; same thing with Hartford," he said.
